activities.caption: fill the blanks — Kant's paradox
activities.name: aesthKantCloze

config.text: Kant's paradox founds the field: judgments of beauty are %%0%% — grounded in a feeling of pleasure, not concepts — yet claim %%1%% assent: anyone who disagrees is invited to look again, not merely dismissed as different.
config.hint: The ground is a feeling; the demand is on everyone.

activities.anchor: The twentieth century broke every definition at once, with a urinal
activities.caption: pair each theory of art with its casualty
activities.name: aesthTheoriesMatch

config.prompt: Four theories, four casualties — pair each theory with what breaks it:

pairs.right: abstract painting and music represent nothing — a perfect photograph need not be art
instrumental music without felt content and cold conceptual art strain it
cannot say why a forgery of perfect form feels lesser, or why context changes everything
explains how anything can be art and nothing about which art is good — definition and evaluation come apart

config.why: Duchamp's Fountain (1917) looks exactly like plumbing and is a pivotal artwork — Weitz's open concept and family resemblance hold what the definitions drop.

activities.caption: true or false — the force of aesthetic judgment
activities.name: aesthNormJudge

statements.s: Judgments of beauty command agreement rather than merely reporting a feeling.
statements.why: They carry normative force — and they are criticisable by reasons: composition, technique, attention to detail.

statements.s: Because standards are contestable, aesthetic argument is pointless.
statements.why: The disagreement is real, but so is the standard — what the standard is exactly remains the open question.

statements.s: Weitz held that "art" is an open concept unified by family resemblance.
statements.why: Overlapping threads — form, expression, representation, craft — rather than a definition.

activities.anchor: The debate has acquired an unplanned laboratory
activities.caption: rebuild the intention debate, step by step
activities.name: aesthIntentOrder

config.prompt: Rebuild the intention debate in order:
items: The intentional fallacy (1946): intentions are private evidence — the work belongs to language and its readers
Death of the author (1967): meaning is made in reading, by culture
The actual intentionalist counter: utterance meaning follows intention everywhere else
Hypothetical intentionalism: what an informed ideal author would most plausibly mean
The laboratory nobody ordered: generative AI makes works with no human intent at the object level
config.why: Intentions are evidence, not verdicts — real ones inform the hypothetical ideal author without deciding.

activities.caption: walk the paradoxes — fiction, then horror
activities.name: aesthFictionBranch

config.root: Two paradoxes run on the same machinery. Walk them.

start.text: You weep for Anna Karenina — and know she does not exist. What is the emotion?

choices.label: Quasi-emotion — you imagine the fear, Walton's make-believe
choices.feedback: Fiction games run the machinery of emotion offline — belief in the object is not required.

choices.label: Real emotion — imagination runs the same machinery as belief
choices.feedback: The cognitive view: the same machinery, only offline.

walton.text: Coleridge's "willing suspension of disbelief" is the older cousin of the same thought.

choices.label: Now the other puzzle — why seek out despairing novels and slasher films?

cog.text: Either way the paradox stands: fear seems to require belief in danger, yet the tears are real.

choices.label: Now the other puzzle — why seek out despairing novels and slasher films?

horror.text: Aristotle's catharsis, Hume's conversion (the beauty of the representation transforms the pain), and the safe-context account: negative emotion plus safety and control equals rehearsal and pleasure — the mechanism behind spicy food and rollercoasters.

config.why: Fiction is not a marginal case — it reveals how emotion generally works, run by imagination.

activities.caption: drag the divider — Hume versus Bourdieu on taste
activities.name: aesthTasteCompare

config.prompt: Drag the divider — the productive tension:

before.label: Hume: standards exist
before.text: Taste can be refined — practice, comparison, freedom from prejudice — and ideal critics converge; their verdicts are the standard, like wine-judging.

after.label: Bourdieu: standards are power
after.text: Taste is habitus — class-trained disposition; "pure" aesthetic judgment is the taste of those who can afford distance from necessity, and universal taste launders social position.

config.why: Both partly right: expertise demonstrably converges, and the canon was demonstrably built under conditions of exclusion — keep both.

config.prompt: File each position in the art-and-morality debate:
buckets: moralism and ethicism — defects can transfer

items.label: Riefenstahl's Triumph of the Will: formally brilliant and morally monstrous, nothing contradictory
aesthetic and ethical value live on separate axes
a work that asks you to admire cruelty as admirable is aesthetically as well as morally worse
Gaut's ethicism: moderate moral flaws are pro tanto aesthetic flaws

config.why: The debate decides real cases: editing problematic classics, enjoying transgressive art, and whether "separating the art from the artist" is coherent.
